overview: This bill, the Legacy Mine Cleanup Act, creates an Office of Mountains, Deserts, and Plains inside the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to coordinate cleanup of land and water polluted by past hardrock mining, such as old gold, silver, copper and uranium mines. The office would bring together EPA headquarters, regional offices, other federal agencies, states, tribes, nonprofits and mining companies, share best practices, and encourage small businesses to take part in cleanup work. Each year the EPA would publish a list of priority mine sites and report to Congress on how cleanup is going. It also requires a 10-year federal plan, first due by September 30, 2028, for cleaning up abandoned uranium mines on Navajo Nation land, and directs the EPA to offer technical help to states, local governments and tribes. The bill does not give the EPA any new regulatory power. The Senate passed it, and as of November 20, 2025, it was being held at the House desk awaiting action.
for: Supporters say thousands of abandoned mines still pollute water in Western and tribal communities, and a single office with a priority list and a Navajo uranium plan would speed up long-delayed cleanups.
against: Critics say the bill creates a new office without providing funding for actual cleanup, so it may add coordination and paperwork without fixing many more sites.
